title: The Hindenburg
subtitle: Thirty-four seconds that ended an age

sections.name: Cold open
lines: title

lines.title: HINDENBURG
lines.sub: Thirty-four seconds that ended an age

lines: At about twenty-five past seven in the evening, on the sixth of May, 1937, the largest aircraft ever built was coming in to land at Lakehurst, New Jersey.
airship
Mooring lines had been dropped to the ground crew below. Reporters and newsreel cameras were waiting. Families of passengers were watching from the edge of the field.
airship
Then a small flame appeared near the tail. In the next half minute or so, the whole ship was consumed by fire.
airship
It fell to the ground, burning, nose up, as people inside jumped or were thrown from its windows.
stat

lines.label: people killed · 62 of the 97 aboard survived

lines: Thirty-six people died. Remarkably, sixty-two of the ninety-seven people on board survived. But the age of the passenger airship died with the Hindenburg that evening.

sections.name: The giant
lines: airship

The Hindenburg was a German airship, a rigid zeppelin, built by the Zeppelin company and launched in 1936. It was two hundred and forty-five metres long, more than three times the length of a modern jumbo jet.
cells

Inside its aluminium frame were sixteen enormous gas bags, holding about seven million cubic feet of hydrogen. That was what lifted it. Hydrogen is the lightest gas there is. It is also extremely flammable.
lesson

lines.text: It was designed to use helium.

lines: The ship had originally been designed to use helium, which is almost as light, and does not burn. But almost all of the world's helium came from the United States, and American law restricted its export. Germany could not get enough.
lesson

lines.text: The ship carried the symbols of the Nazi state.

lines: By the 1930s, the Zeppelin company had been taken under the influence of Hitler's government, and the Hindenburg carried the swastika on its tail fins. It was a flying piece of national prestige.
people
On board, it was a luxury liner. There were cabins, a dining room, a lounge, promenade decks with sloping windows, and even a pressurised smoking room, sealed off from the hydrogen above.
map

In its first season, 1936, it made seventeen round trips across the Atlantic without serious incident, to North America and to Brazil. Crossing took about two to three days, much faster than an ocean liner.

sections.name: The last voyage
lines: date

lines.place: Frankfurt · first North American crossing of the season

lines: On the third of May, 1937, the Hindenburg left Frankfurt on its first North American trip of the new season. It carried thirty-six passengers and sixty-one crew.
portrait
It was commanded by Captain Max Pruss. Also on board was Ernst Lehmann, one of Germany's most experienced airship captains, travelling as an observer.
airship

Strong headwinds slowed the crossing. When the ship reached the American coast on the afternoon of the sixth of May, it was already behind schedule. It flew over Manhattan, where crowds came out to watch.
airship

lines.label: waiting off the coast for the storms to pass

lines: Then the weather turned. Thunderstorms were passing over the naval air station at Lakehurst. The landing was delayed while the Hindenburg waited off the coast for them to clear.
airship
By early evening, the storm had moved through, but the air was still damp and electrically charged. The ship came in to land, with orders to hurry.

sections.name: The landing
lines: airship

lines.label: a sharp turn on the approach

lines: On the final approach, the Hindenburg made a sharp turn to line up with the mooring mast. To trim the ship, the crew released water ballast from the front, and valved off hydrogen from the back.
airship
At around seven twenty-one, the mooring lines were dropped from the nose. Ground crew grabbed them. The ship hung about two hundred feet in the air.
people

lines.label: a flicker of flame near the tail

lines: A few minutes later, some witnesses saw something like a ripple in the fabric near the top of the tail, or a faint blue glow. Then a burst of flame appeared just ahead of the upper fin.
clock
It was about twenty-five past seven.
airship
The fire spread forward through the hydrogen cells with terrifying speed. The tail, losing lift, dropped. The nose pointed up.
airship
In roughly thirty-two to thirty-seven seconds, depending on who measured it, the ship went from first flame to a burning wreck on the ground.

sections.name: Thirty-four seconds
lines: people

Inside, people had only seconds to react. Some passengers jumped from the windows of the promenade deck as the ship came down. Those who jumped from low enough often survived. Those who jumped too early, from too high, did not.
people

One family was in the dining room. As the ship neared the ground, the mother threw her two sons out of a window, and then jumped herself. All three survived, though the boys' father and sister did not. The younger boy, eight-year-old Werner Doehner, was the last living survivor of the Hindenburg until he died in 2019.
people

lines.label: ground crew ran towards the fire

lines: On the ground, members of the naval ground crew ran towards the burning wreck to pull people out. One of them, Allen Hagaman, was killed.
stat

lines.label: 13 passengers · 22 crew · 1 member of the ground crew

lines: Thirteen passengers and twenty-two crew members died, along with Hagaman. Ernst Lehmann was carried out alive, badly burned. He died the next day.

sections.name: Oh, the humanity
lines: portrait
Among the reporters at Lakehurst was Herbert Morrison, from a Chicago radio station, recording a report on disc to be broadcast the next day.
quote

lines.text: It's burst into flames! … Oh, the humanity!

lines: His voice, breaking as he watched the ship burn, became one of the most famous recordings ever made. It's burst into flames, he cried, and then, oh, the humanity.
lesson

lines.text: For the first time, the world watched a disaster.

lines: Newsreel cameras filmed the whole thing. Within days, audiences in cinemas around the world watched the Hindenburg burn. It was one of the first great disasters that the public could see with their own eyes.

sections.name: What happened
lines: inquiry

lines.label: US Commerce Department and German inquiries · 1937

lines: American and German investigators reached broadly the same conclusion. Hydrogen had been leaking somewhere near the tail, perhaps from a gas cell damaged during the sharp turn. And something had ignited it.
cells

lines.label: leaking hydrogen + a spark of static electricity

lines: The most likely spark was static electricity. The ship had flown through charged, stormy air. When its wet mooring lines touched the ground, the frame was earthed, but parts of the outer skin may not have been. A discharge could have jumped across.
lesson

lines.text: There was no evidence of sabotage.

lines: Theories of sabotage, popular at the time, were never supported by evidence. Later researchers have argued about how much the ship's coated fabric skin helped the fire spread. But without the hydrogen, there would have been no disaster.

sections.name: The end of an age
lines: timeline
A flammable lifting gas, used because the safe one was unavailable. A ship behind schedule. A hurried landing in charged air after a storm. A sharp turn that may have opened a leak.
lesson

lines.text: Public trust in airships was gone.

lines: The airship industry never recovered. Its sister ship was finished, but never carried paying passengers. The older Graf Zeppelin was retired. Within a few years, the first commercial aeroplanes were flying the Atlantic.
lesson
Statistically, airships had a reasonable safety record for their time. But one fire, caught on film, was enough to end them. Public confidence, once lost in thirty-four seconds, could not be rebuilt.
lesson

The engineers had always known that hydrogen was dangerous. They had planned around it, with rules, procedures and care. For years, it worked. Then, on a stormy evening, behind schedule, all the conditions came together at once.
memorial
Today, a marker on the field at Lakehurst shows where the Hindenburg came down.
